science.title: TransAct: efficient attention-based temporal modelling for real-time wearable human activity recognition
science.description: Wearable sensors have made Human Activity Recognition (HAR) via intelligent healthcare and assisted living systems very efficient by enabling the quick processing of multivariate time-series streams of data. We propose a novel framework known as TransAct that utilizes a Transformer-based architecture for the computationally efficient temporal modeling of wearable sensor signals. TransAct is designed to capture long-range dependencies among sensor-derived features by leveraging optimized input projection, learnable positional encodings, and multi-headed self-attention mechanisms. We construct a hybrid CNN-LSTM architecture as a matched comparator, applying identical preprocessing and training configuration to both models, and evaluate both across five independent random seeds on three public benchmarks: UCI HAR, PAMAP2, and OPPORTUNITY. On UCI HAR, TransAct shows a higher held-out test accuracy than the CNN-LSTM baseline ($$95.10\% \pm 0.37\%$$ vs. $$94.26\% \pm 0.55\%$$), a borderline-significant advantage by a paired t-test ($$p=0.050$$) that does not reach significance under the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test ($$p=0.125$$). On PAMAP2, where the input is genuine chronologically-ordered raw inertial signal rather than UCI HAR’s reshaped engineered-feature vector, the advantage is larger and more clearly significant ($$86.13\% \pm 0.68\%$$ vs. $$82.75\% \pm 1.70\%$$; $$p=0.012$$). On OPPORTUNITY, a severely class-imbalanced 18-class gesture-recognition benchmark, overall accuracy is statistically indistinguishable between the two models ($$88.48\% \pm 3.54\%$$ vs. $$89.01\% \pm 2.64\%$$; $$p=0.452$$), but TransAct achieves significantly higher macro-F1 ($$54.15\% \pm 9.17\%$$ vs. $$51.55\% \pm 9.04\%$$; $$p=0.030$$), the more informative metric under severe class imbalance since it does not let performance on the dominant “Null” class dominate the score. A multi-seed ablation study on UCI HAR finds no statistically detectable contribution from any of the three architectural components tested individually – positional encoding, multi-head (vs. single-head) attention, and layer normalization all leave accuracy statistically indistinguishable from the full model ($$p>0.9$$ in every case). TransAct is consistently and significantly slower than the CNN-LSTM baseline across all three datasets: on a T4 GPU, mean epoch time and per-sample inference latency are both roughly 2–3$$\times$$ higher for TransAct than for CNN-LSTM ($$p<0.0001$$ throughout), consistent with TransAct’s larger parameter count. Taken together, these results support a specific and dataset-dependent conclusion: attention-based modeling of engineered or raw wearable-sensor sequences yields a real, reproducible accuracy or macro-F1 advantage over a matched recurrent baseline on two of the three benchmarks tested, most clearly on genuine time-series input, but this advantage is not universal (it does not appear in OPPORTUNITY’s overall accuracy), and it always comes at a genuine, non-trivial, and consistent computational cost. We report these results, including the null and negative findings, alongside the accuracy gains, and discuss what remains to be established (probability-calibrated discrimination curves, a resolved discrepancy in our OPPORTUNITY channel count, and a mechanistic account of the ablation null results) before broader claims of efficiency or component-level necessity can be supported.

science.title: Desmin filaments extend along actin filaments within the mouse skeletal muscle sarcomere
science.description: Although desmin intermediate filaments are critical for muscle architecture and homeostasis, their spatial 3D organization remains elusive. Their known localization to sarcomeric Z-lines delimits the periodic array of actin and myosin filaments. Here, using dSTORM and SIM sub-diffraction resolution microscopy, we resolve the spatial 3D organization of desmin filaments within mouse skeletal muscle, and reveal they are not confined to Z-lines. Our reconstruction reveals that desmin intermediate filaments extend from Z-lines into the sarcomere interior, where they align with actin filaments. Functional assays show that disrupting desmin filament assembly in normal male mouse muscle using a dominant negative inhibitor of desmin selectively reduces active tension at longer sarcomere lengths, indicating a role for desmin in sarcomere mechanics. These findings expand the structural model of the muscle sarcomere and support a role for desmin in force production. Here, the authors use super-resolution microscopy to show that desmin filaments extend beyond Z-lines and align with actin inside mouse skeletal muscle sarcomeres, where they help support force generation when sarcomeres are stretched.
